subChunks.title: Comparator, Method References & Functional Composition
subChunks.hookHtml: You have used lambdas to write predicates and map functions. Now you will wield them as first-class values — passing Comparators into sorts, composing multiple functions into pipelines, and eliminating boilerplate with method references.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Comparator with Lambdas

Comparator.comparing() and chained comparators replace verbose anonymous classes:

List<String> spells = Arrays.asList("Fireball", "Ice", "Thunder", "Arc");

// Sort by length
spells.sort(Comparator.comparingInt(String::length));

// Sort by length, then alphabetically
spells.sort(Comparator.comparingInt(String::length)
                      .thenComparing(Comparator.naturalOrder()));

// Reverse
spells.sort(Comparator.comparingInt(String::length).reversed());

Method References

Method references are shorthand for lambdas that do nothing but call a method:

// Lambda                         Method reference
str -> str.toUpperCase()          String::toUpperCase
n   -> Math.abs(n)                Math::abs
s   -> System.out.println(s)      System.out::println
() -> new ArrayList<>()          ArrayList::new

List<String> names = List.of("lyria", "kira", "vey");
names.stream()
     .map(String::toUpperCase)       // instance method ref
     .forEach(System.out::println);  // instance method ref on object

Four kinds: ClassName::staticMethod, ClassName::instanceMethod (called on the argument), object::instanceMethod (called on a specific object), ClassName::new (constructor).

Functional Composition

Function<T,R> has andThen() and compose() to chain transformations:

Function<String, String> trim   = String::trim;
Function<String, String> upper  = String::toUpperCase;
Function<String, Integer> len   = String::length;

Function<String, String> clean = trim.andThen(upper);
System.out.println(clean.apply("  fireball  ")); // FIREBALL

Function<String, Integer> cleanLen = trim.andThen(upper).andThen(len);
System.out.println(cleanLen.apply("  hi  ")); // 2

Predicate Composition

Predicate<Integer> positive  = n -> n > 0;
Predicate<Integer> even      = n -> n % 2 == 0;
Predicate<Integer> posEven   = positive.and(even);
Predicate<Integer> posOrEven = positive.or(even);
Predicate<Integer> negative  = positive.negate();

posEven.test(4);   // true
posEven.test(-4);  // false

storyBeats.text: The Academy's spell library has thousands of entries. An apprentice attempts to sort them — by power, then by name, then in reverse. Three separate sort calls, each with a different anonymous class. The senior enchanter watching shakes her head slowly.

storyBeats.speaker: Enchantress Vera
storyBeats.text: You have learned lambdas. Now use them properly. Comparator.comparing() chains. Method references eliminate the noise. Functional composition builds pipelines. One line does the work of twenty.

storyBeats.speaker: Enchantress Vera
storyBeats.text: Method references are lambdas with the noise stripped. If your lambda does nothing but call one method, write the method reference instead. String::toUpperCase instead of s -> s.toUpperCase(). Four forms — static, instance-on-argument, instance-on-specific-object, constructor.

storyBeats.speaker: Function composition pipeline
storyBeats.text:
Function<String, Integer> pipeline =
    ((Function<String, String>) String::trim)
    .andThen(String::toUpperCase)
    .andThen(String::length);

System.out.println(pipeline.apply("  Arcane  ")); // 6

learningObjectives: Use Comparator.comparingInt(), thenComparing(), and reversed() to compose sort orders
Write method references for all four forms: static, unbound instance, bound instance, constructor
Compose two Function instances with andThen() to build a transformation pipeline
Combine Predicates with and(), or(), and negate()
commonMistakes: Using object::method when you want ClassName::method — the former captures a specific object, the latter is called on each stream element
Forgetting that andThen(f).andThen(g) applies f first, then g — compose() is the reverse order
Trying to use method references for methods that take multiple parameters — the functional interface must match the arity
Ignoring the type inference — sometimes a cast or explicit type is needed for method reference chains
assessmentCriteria: Can sort a List<T> by multiple fields using a chained Comparator without anonymous classes
Can identify which of the four method reference forms applies to a given lambda
Can build a multi-step Function pipeline and predict its output
Can compose two Predicates with and() and explain the difference from writing a single combined lambda
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain method references — what they are, the four forms, and when to use each. Then explain functional composition with andThen() — what problem does it solve compared to just nesting method calls?
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Given a list of spells (represented as Strings), perform the following operations:

  1. Sort by length ascending, then alphabetically for equal lengths. Print the sorted list.
  2. Using a Function pipeline: trim, upper-case, and take the length of each spell name. Print the result for " frostbolt ".
  3. Compose a Predicate that is true when a spell name has length > 4 AND starts with 'F'. Filter the list and print matches.

guidedPracticeTests.label: Filtered spells (length>4 and starts with F)

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
From scratch. Given List<Integer> nums = Arrays.asList(3, -1, 8, -4, 2, 7, -3, 6):

  • Use a composed Predicate (positive AND even) to filter and print matching elements
  • Sort the list in descending order using a lambda Comparator
  • Create a Function<Integer, String> pipeline that converts a number to its absolute value then to a String with suffix "pts". Apply it to each element of the original list and collect to a new list, then print it.

questions.explanation: String::toUpperCase is an unbound instance method reference — the method is called on whichever String is provided as the argument. Contrast with someString::toUpperCase (bound — always called on someString).

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between f.andThen(g) and f.compose(g)?
options: andThen applies f first then g; compose applies g first then f
compose applies f first then g; andThen applies g first then f
They are identical — both apply f then g
compose only works on Predicate, andThen only works on Function
questions.answer: andThen applies f first then g; compose applies g first then f
questions.explanation: f.andThen(g) = g(f(x)). f.compose(g) = f(g(x)). So trim.andThen(upper) trims then uppercases, while trim.compose(upper) uppercases first then trims.
